Darcy’s law and diffusion for a two-fluid Euler-Maxwell system with dissipation

Renjun Duan Address: (RJD) Department of Mathematics, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shatin, Hong Kong Email address: rjduan@math.cuhk.edu.hk , Qingqing Liu Address: (QQL) The Hubei Key Laboratory of Mathematical Physics, School of Mathematics and Statistics, Central China Normal University, Wuhan, 430079, P. R. China Email address: shuxueliuqingqing@126.com and Changjiang Zhu Address: (CJZ) The Hubei Key Laboratory of Mathematical Physics, School of Mathematics and Statistics, Central China Normal University, Wuhan, 430079, P. R. China Email address: cjzhu@mail.ccnu.edu.cn
Abstract.

This paper is concerned with the large-time behavior of solutions to the Cauchy problem on the two-fluid Euler-Maxwell system with dissipation when initial data are around a constant equilibrium state. The main goal is the rigorous justification of diffusion phenomena in fluid plasma at the linear level. Precisely, motivated by the classical Darcy’s law for the nonconductive fluid, we first give a heuristic derivation of the asymptotic equations of the Euler-Maxwell system in large time. It turns out that both the density and the magnetic field tend time-asymptotically to the diffusion equations with diffusive coefficients explicitly determined by given physical parameters. Then, in terms of the Fourier energy method, we analyze the linear dissipative structure of the system, which implies the almost exponential time-decay property of solutions over the high-frequency domain. The key part of the paper is the spectral analysis of the linearized system, exactly capturing the diffusive feature of solutions over the low-frequency domain. Finally, under some conditions on initial data, we show the convergence of the densities and the magnetic field to the corresponding linear diffusion waves with the rate (1+t)−5/4(1+t)^{-5/4} in L2L^{2} norm and also the convergence of the velocities and the electric field to the corresponding asymptotic profiles given in the sense of the geneneralized Darcy’s law with the faster rate (1+t)−7/4(1+t)^{-7/4} in L2L^{2} norm. Thus, this work can be also regarded as the mathematical proof of the Darcy’s law in the context of collisional fluid plasma.

Key words and phrases: 
Euler-Maxwell system; dissipation; diffusion waves; large-time behavior

1. Introduction

It is generally believed that the Darcy’s law governs the motion of the inviscid flow with frictional damping [27] or the slow viscous flow [25] in large time. It is quite nontrivial to mathematically justify the large-time behavior of solutions to those relative physical systems, particularly in the case when vacuum appears, cf. [4, 19, 28, 29]. Besides, there are also some results, for instance, see [21] and references therein, to discuss the modified Darcy’s law for conducting porous media. In the paper, we attempt to give a rigorous proof of Darcy’s laws and diffusion phenomena in the context of collisional fluid plasma whenever the densities of fluids are close to non-vacuum states.

In a weakly ionised gas with a small enough ionisation fraction, charged particles will interact primarily by means of elastic collisions with neutral atoms rather than with other charged particles, cf. [13, Chapter 12.4]. In such situation, the motion of fluid plasmas consisting of ions (α=i)(\alpha=i), electrons (α=e)(\alpha=e) and neutral atoms is generally governed by the two-fluid Euler-Maxwell system in three space dimensions

{∂tnα+∇⋅(nα​uα)=0,mα​nα​(∂tuα+uα⋅∇uα)+∇pα​(nα)=qα​nα​(E+uαc×B)−να​mα​nα​uα,∂tE−c∇×B=−4π∑α=i,eqαnαuα,∂tB+c∇×E=0,∇⋅E=4π∑α=i,eqαnα,∇⋅B=0.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}n_{\alpha}+\nabla\cdot(n_{\alpha}u_{\alpha})=0,\\ &m_{\alpha}n_{\alpha}(\partial_{t}u_{\alpha}+u_{\alpha}\cdot\nabla u_{\alpha})+\nabla p_{\alpha}(n_{\alpha})\\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad=q_{\alpha}n_{\alpha}\left(E+\frac{u_{\alpha}}{c}\times B\right)-\nu_{\alpha}m_{\alpha}n_{\alpha}u_{\alpha},\\ &\partial_{t}E-c\nabla\times B=-4\pi\sum_{\alpha=i,e}q_{\alpha}n_{\alpha}u_{\alpha},\\ &\partial_{t}B+c\nabla\times E=0,\\ &\nabla\cdot E=4\pi\sum_{\alpha=i,e}q_{\alpha}n_{\alpha},\ \ \nabla\cdot B=0.\end{aligned}\right. (1.1)

The paper is concerned with the large-time asymptotic behavior of solutions to the Cauchy problem on the two-fluid Euler-Maxwell system with collisions whenever initial data are close to a constant equilibrium state [nα=1,uα=0,E=0,B=0][n_{\alpha}=1,u_{\alpha}=0,E=0,B=0]. Notice that collision terms play a key role in the analysis of the problem, see [33] for instance. For that purpose, we introduce the large-time asymptotic profile as follows. Let Gμ(t,x)=(4πμt)−3/2exp{−|x|2/(4μt)}G_{\mu}(t,x)=(4\pi\mu t)^{-3/2}\exp\{-|x|^{2}/(4\mu t)\} be the heat kernel with the diffusion coefficient μ>0\mu>0. Let us define the ambipolar diffusive coefficient μ1>0\mu_{1}>0 and the magnetic diffusive coefficient μ2>0\mu_{2}>0 by

μ1=Ti+Temi​νi+me​νe,μ2=c2​mi​νi​me​νe4​π​e2​(mi​νi+me​νe),\displaystyle\mu_{1}=\frac{T_{i}+T_{e}}{m_{i}\nu_{i}+m_{e}\nu_{e}},\quad\mu_{2}=\frac{c^{2}m_{i}\nu_{i}m_{e}\nu_{e}}{4\pi e^{2}\left(m_{i}\nu_{i}+m_{e}\nu_{e}\right)}, (1.4)

(1.8)

The main result of the paper is stated as follows.

Theorem 1.1.

There are constants ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and C>0C>0 such that if

∑α=i,e‖[nα​0−1,uα​0]‖H11∩L1+‖[E0,B0]‖H11∩L1<ϵ,\sum_{\alpha=i,e}\|[n_{\alpha 0}-1,u_{\alpha 0}]\|_{H^{11}\cap L^{1}}+\|[E_{0},B_{0}]\|_{H^{11}\cap L^{1}}<\epsilon, (1.9)

then the Cauchy problem (1.1), (1.2), (1.3) admits a unique global solution

nα−1,uα,E,B∈C⁡([0,∞),H5​(ℝ3)),n_{\alpha}-1,u_{\alpha},E,B\in C([0,\infty);H^{5}(\mathbb{R}^{3})), (1.10)

satisfying

∑α=i,e‖nα−1−n¯‖L2+‖B−B¯‖L2≤C​(1+t)−54,\sum_{\alpha=i,e}\|n_{\alpha}-1-\overline{n}\|_{L^{2}}+\|B-\overline{B}\|_{L^{2}}\leq C(1+t)^{-\frac{5}{4}}, (1.11)

and

∑α=i,e‖uα−u¯α‖L2+‖E−E¯‖L2≤C​(1+t)−74,\sum_{\alpha=i,e}\|u_{\alpha}-\overline{u}_{\alpha}\|_{L^{2}}+\|E-\overline{E}\|_{L^{2}}\leq C(1+t)^{-\frac{7}{4}}, (1.12)

for all t≥0t\geq 0.

We give a few remarks on Theorem 1.1. First of all, from the proof later on, under the assumption (1.9) the solution to the Cauchy problem (1.1), (1.2), (1.3) around the constant equilibrium state enjoys the time-decay property

∑α=i,e‖[nα−1,uα]‖L2+‖[E,B]‖L2≤C​(1+t)−34,\sum_{\alpha=i,e}\|[n_{\alpha}-1,u_{\alpha}]\|_{L^{2}}+\|[E,B]\|_{L^{2}}\leq C(1+t)^{-\frac{3}{4}},

where the time-decay rate must be optimal for general initial data with B0≠0B_{0}\neq 0 due to those results from the spectral analysis given in Section 4; see Corollary 4.2 for instance. On the other hand the large-time asymptotic profile also satisfies

‖n¯‖L2+‖B¯‖L2≤C​(1+t)−34,∑α=i,e‖u¯α‖L2+‖E¯‖L2≤C​(1+t)−54,\|\overline{n}\|_{L^{2}}+\|\overline{B}\|_{L^{2}}\leq C(1+t)^{-\frac{3}{4}},\quad\sum_{\alpha=i,e}\|\overline{u}_{\alpha}\|_{L^{2}}+\|\overline{E}\|_{L^{2}}\leq C(1+t)^{-\frac{5}{4}},

which are also optimal in terms of the definition (1.5), (1.6), (1.7), (1.8) of [n¯,u¯α,E¯,B¯][\overline{n},\overline{u}_{\alpha},\overline{E},\overline{B}]. Therefore it is nontrivial to obtain the faster time-decay rates (1.11) and (1.12), and this also assures that [1+n¯,u¯α,E¯,B¯][1+\overline{n},\overline{u}_{\alpha},\overline{E},\overline{B}] indeed can be regarded as the more accurate large-time asymptotic profile for solutions to the Cauchy problem under consideration, compared to the trivial constant equilibrium state. Notice that n¯\overline{n} and B¯\overline{B} are diffusion waves by (1.5) and (1.6) as well as (1.4), and u¯α\overline{u}_{\alpha} and E¯\overline{E} are defined in terms of those two diffusion waves by (1.7) and (1.8). From the heuristic derivation of the large-time asymptotic profiles in the next section, we see that the asymptotic profiles can be solved from the asymptotic equations obtained in a formal way in the sense of the Darcy’s law. In the case without any electromagnetic field, there have been extensive mathematical studies of the large-time behavior for the damped Euler system basing on the Darcy’s law; see [11, 18, 28, 29] and reference therein. However few rigorous results are known for such physical law in the context of two-fluid plasma with collisions. This work can be regarded to some extent as the generalisation of the Darcy’s law for the classical non-conductive fluid to the plasma fluid under the influence of the self-consistent electromagnetic field.

Second, by (1.9) and (1.10), there is a discrepancy between regularities of initial data and the solution. The reason for the discrepancy is that the Euler-Maxwell with collisions is of the regularity-loss type, which is essentially induced by the fact that eigenvalues of the linearized system may tend asymptotically to the imaginary axis as the frequency goes to infinity; see [6] in the one-fluid case. There has been a general theory developed in [36] in terms of the Fourier energy method to study the decay structure of general symmetric hyperbolic systems with partial relaxations of the regularity-loss type. The main feature of time-decay properties for such regularity-loss system is that solutions over the high-frequency domain can still gain the enough time-decay rate by compensating enough regularity of initial data.

Third, the key point of Theorem 1.1 is to present the convergence in L2L^{2} norm of the solution [nα,uα,E,B][n_{\alpha},u_{\alpha},E,B] to the profile [1+n¯,u¯α,E¯,B¯][1+\overline{n},\overline{u}_{\alpha},\overline{E},\overline{B}] if initial data approach the constant steady state in the sense of (1.9). There could be several direct generalisations of the current result. As in [37], it can be expected to obtain the convergence rates for the derivatives up to to some order. In general, the higher the order of derivatives is, the faster they decay in time. Another possible approach for obtaining the global existence and convergence of solutions to the constant steady state is to introduce as in [15] the negative Sobolev space basing on the pure energy method together with the functional interpolation inequalities, where the advantage is that both L2L^{2} norms of the higher derivatives and L1L^{1} norms of the zero-order are not necessarily small. However, it seems still nontrivial to apply such method to obtain the large-time asymptotic behaviour (1.11) and (1.12).

The final remark is concerned with the nonlinear diffusion of the two fluid Euler-Maxwell system with collisions. In fact, the current work is done at the linearized level. Even for the general pressure functions PαP_{\alpha} (α=i,e)(\alpha=i,e), by using the same formal derivation as in Section 2, the density satisfies the nonlinear heat equation

∂tn¯−Δ​P​(n¯)=0,\partial_{t}\overline{n}-\Delta P(\overline{n})=0,

where P⁡(⋅)P(\cdot) is in connection with PαP_{\alpha} (α=i,e)(\alpha=i,e) as well as other physical parameters. The nonlinear heat equation above is also a type of the porous medium equation. Thus, it would be interesting and challenging to further investigate the asymptotic stability of the nonlinear diffusion waves, cf. [18]. We hope to report it in the future study.

To prove Theorem 1.1 we need to carry out the spectral analysis of the linearized system around the constant steady state; see [26], for instance. In fact, the solution can be written as the sum of the fluid part and the electromagnetic part in the form of

[ρα​(t,x)uα​(t,x)E⁡(t,x)B⁡(t,x)]=[ρα​(t,x)uα,∥(t,x)E∥​(t,x)0]+[0uα,⟂​(t,x)E⟂​(t,x)B⁡(t,x)].\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\rho_{\alpha}(t,x)\\ u_{\alpha}(t,x)\\ E(t,x)\\ B(t,x)\\ \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\rho_{\alpha}(t,x)\\ u_{\alpha,\parallel}(t,x)\\ E_{\parallel}(t,x)\\ 0\\ \end{array}\right]+\left[\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ u_{\alpha,\perp}(t,x)\\ E_{\perp}(t,x)\\ B(t,x)\\ \end{array}\right].

However it seems difficult to give an explicit representation of solutions to two eigenvalue problems due to the high phase dimensions under consideration. The main idea is to obtain the asymptotic expansions of solutions to the linearized system as the frequency |k|→0|k|\to 0 (cf. [7], [20]); see Section 4. One trick to deal with the electromagnetic part is to first reduce the system to the high-order ODE of the magnetic field BB only, then study the asymptotic expansion of BB as |k|→0|k|\to 0, and finally apply the Fourier energy method to estimate the other two components uα,⟂u_{\alpha,\perp} and E⟂E_{\perp}(cf. [10] and reference therein); see Lemma 4.4. For |k|→∞|k|\to\infty, it can be directly treated by the Fourier energy method since the linearized solution operator in the Fourier space behaves like

exp⁡{−λ​|k|2(1+|k|2)2​t},\exp\left\{-\frac{\lambda|k|^{2}}{(1+|k|^{2})^{2}}t\right\},

which leads to the almost exponential time-decay depending on regularity of initial data; see Section 3. In the mean time, we find that the large-time behavior of solutions to the two-fluid Euler-Maxwell system (1.1) is governed by the following two subsystems

{∂tn+∇⋅(n​u∥)=0,∇Pα(n)=qαnE∥−ναmαnu∥,α=i,e,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle\partial_{t}n+\nabla\cdot(nu_{\parallel})=0,\\[8.53581pt] \displaystyle\nabla P_{\alpha}(n)=q_{\alpha}nE_{\parallel}-\nu_{\alpha}m_{\alpha}nu_{\parallel},\quad\alpha=i,e,\end{array}\right.

and

{qαE⟂−ναmαuα,⟂=0,α=i,e,−c∇×B=−4πn∑α=i,eqαuα,⟂,∂tB+c∇×E⟂=0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle q_{\alpha}E_{\perp}-\nu_{\alpha}m_{\alpha}u_{\alpha,\perp}=0,\quad\alpha=i,e,\\[8.53581pt] \displaystyle-c\nabla\times B=-4\pi n\sum_{\alpha=i,e}q_{\alpha}u_{\alpha,\perp},\\[8.53581pt] \displaystyle\partial_{t}B+c\nabla\times E_{\perp}=0.\end{array}\right.

For more details see Section 2 and Section 4.

Finally we would mention the following works related to the paper: some derivations and numerical computations of the relative models [1, 2, 5, 35], global existence and large-time behavior for the damped Euler-Maxwell system [3, 6, 8, 30, 32, 34, 37, 38, 39, 40], global existence in the non-damping case [12, 14, 22], and asymptotic limits under small parameters [16, 31, 32].

The rest of the paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, we give the heuristic derivation of diffusion waves motivated by the classical Darcy’s law. In Section 3 we reformulate the Cauchy problem on the Euler-Maxwell system around the constant steady state, and study the decay structure of the linearized homogeneous system by the Fourier energy method. In Section 4, we present the spectral analysis of the linearized system by three parts. The fist part is for the fluid, the second one for the electromagnetic field, and the third one for the extra time-decay of solutions with special initial data. The result in the third part accounts for estimating the inhomogeneous source terms. In Section 5, we first prove the global existence of solutions by the energy method, show the time asymptotic rate of solutions around the constant states and then obtain the main result concerning the time asymptotic rate around linear diffusion waves.

2. Heuristic derivation of diffusion waves

In this section we would provide a heuristic derivation of the large-time asymptotic equations of the densities, velocities and the electromagnetic field. Indeed, both the densities and the magnetic field satisfy the diffusion equations with different diffusion coefficients in terms of those physical parameters appearing in the system, and the velocities and the electric field are defined by the densities and the magnetic field according to the Darcy’s law.

2.1. Diffusion of densities

We first give a formal derivation of the large-time asymptotic equations of densities and velocities. Assume the quasineutral condition

ni=ne=n⁡(t,x),ui=ue=u⁡(t,x),\displaystyle n_{i}=n_{e}=n(t,x),\quad u_{i}=u_{e}=u(t,x), (2.1)

and also assume that the background magnetic field is a constant vector, for instance, B=(0,0,|B|)B=(0,0,|B|) is constant along x3x_{3}-direction. Note that |B||B| here is not necessarily assumed to be zero.

We start from the asymptotic momentum equations for α=i\alpha=i and ee:

∇pα​(n)=qα​n​(E+uc×B)−να​mα​n​u.\displaystyle\nabla p_{\alpha}(n)=q_{\alpha}n\left(E+\frac{u}{c}\times B\right)-\nu_{\alpha}m_{\alpha}nu. (2.2)

Along BB, (2.2) reduces to

∇pα​(n)⋅B=qα​n​E⋅B−να​mα​n​u⋅B.\displaystyle\nabla p_{\alpha}(n)\cdot B=q_{\alpha}nE\cdot B-\nu_{\alpha}m_{\alpha}nu\cdot B.

i.e.,

{∇pi​(n)⋅B=e​n​E⋅B−νi​mi​n​u⋅B,∇pe(n)⋅B=−enE⋅B−νemenu⋅B.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} &\nabla p_{i}(n)\cdot B=enE\cdot B-\nu_{i}m_{i}nu\cdot B,\\ &\nabla p_{e}(n)\cdot B=-enE\cdot B-\nu_{e}m_{e}nu\cdot B.\end{aligned}\right.

It can be further written in the matrix form:

(∇pi⋅B∇pe⋅B)=(e​n−νi​mi​n−e​n−νe​me​n)​(E⋅Bu⋅B).\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\nabla p_{i}\cdot B\\ \nabla p_{e}\cdot B\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}en&\ -\nu_{i}m_{i}n\\ -en&\ -\nu_{e}m_{e}n\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}E\cdot B\\ u\cdot B\end{array}\right).

One can solve E⋅BE\cdot B and u⋅Bu\cdot B as

2.2. Diffusion of the magnetic field

Notice that the large-time asymptotic profiles of uu and EE given by (2.36) and (2.39) are along the gravitational direction of the diffusive density nn determined by (2.37). Let uα,⟂u_{\alpha,\perp} (α=i,e)(\alpha=i,e) and E⟂E_{\perp} be the asymptotic profiles along the direction normal to the gravitation of the density. Then by taking the background densities as ni=ne=1n_{i}=n_{e}=1, we expect that the large-time profile of the magnetic field BB is governed by the following system

{−e​E⟂+mi​νi​ui,⟂=0,e​E⟂+me​νe​ue,⟂=0,−c∇×B+4π(eui,⟂−eue,⟂)=0,∂tB+c∇×E⟂=0.\left\{\begin{aligned} &-e{E}_{\perp}+m_{i}\nu_{i}{u}_{i,\perp}=0,\\ &e{E}_{\perp}+m_{e}\nu_{e}{u}_{e,\perp}=0,\\ &-c\nabla\times{B}+4\pi(e{u}_{i,\perp}-e{u}_{e,\perp})=0,\\ &\partial_{t}{B}+c\nabla\times{E}_{\perp}=0.\\ \end{aligned}\right.

It is easy to obtain that BB satisfies the diffusion equation

∂tB−c2​mi​νi​me​νe4​π​e2​(mi​νi+me​νe)​Δ​B=0,\partial_{t}{B}-\dfrac{c^{2}m_{i}\nu_{i}m_{e}\nu_{e}}{4\pi e^{2}(m_{i}\nu_{i}+m_{e}\nu_{e})}\Delta B=0,

and uα,⟂u_{\alpha,\perp} (α=i,e)(\alpha=i,e) and E⟂E_{\perp} are given by

{ui,⟂=emi​νiE⟂=c4​π​eme​νemi​νi+me​νe∇×B,ue,⟂=−eme​νeE⟂=−c4​π​emi​νimi​νi+me​νe∇×B,E⟂=c4​π​e2mi​νi​me​νemi​νi+me​νe∇×B.\left\{\begin{aligned} &{u}_{i,\perp}=\frac{e}{m_{i}\nu_{i}}{E}_{\perp}=\frac{c}{4\pi e}\dfrac{m_{e}\nu_{e}}{m_{i}\nu_{i}+m_{e}\nu_{e}}\nabla\times{B},\\ &{u}_{e,\perp}=-\frac{e}{m_{e}\nu_{e}}{E}_{\perp}=-\frac{c}{4\pi e}\dfrac{m_{i}\nu_{i}}{m_{i}\nu_{i}+m_{e}\nu_{e}}\nabla\times{B},\\ &{E}_{\perp}=\frac{c}{4\pi e^{2}}\dfrac{m_{i}\nu_{i}m_{e}\nu_{e}}{m_{i}\nu_{i}+m_{e}\nu_{e}}\nabla\times{B}.\\ \end{aligned}\right.

3. Decay property of linearized system

In this section, we study the time-decay property of solutions to the linearized system basing on the Fourier energy method. The result of this part is similar to the case of one-fluid in [6], and also similar to the study of two-species kinetic Vlasov-Maxwell-Boltzmann system in [9]. The main motivation to present this part is to understand the linear dissipative structure of such complex system as in [36] in terms of the direct energy method and also provide a clue to the more delicate spectral analysis to be given later on. Notice that the key estimate (3.17) in this section will be used to deal with the time-decay property of solutions over the high-frequency domain in the next sections.

3.1. Reformulation of the problem

We assume that the steady state of the Euler-Maxwell system (1.1) is trivial, taking the form of

nα=1,uα=0,E=B=0.n_{\alpha}=1,\ u_{\alpha}=0,\ E=B=0.

Before constructing the more accurate large-time asymptotic profile around the trivial steady state, we first consider the linearized system around the above constant state. For that, let us set ρα=nα−1\rho_{\alpha}=n_{\alpha}-1 for α=i\alpha=i and ee. Then U:=[ρα,uα,E,B]U:=[\rho_{\alpha},u_{\alpha},E,B] satisfies

{∂tρα+∇⋅uα=g1​α,mα∂tuα+Tα∇ρα−qαE+mαναuα=g2​α,∂tE−c∇×B+4π∑α=i,eqαuα=g3,∂tB+c∇×E=0,∇⋅E=4π∑α=i,eqαρα,∇⋅B=0.\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}\rho_{\alpha}+\nabla\cdot u_{\alpha}=g_{1\alpha},\\ &m_{\alpha}\partial_{t}u_{\alpha}+T_{\alpha}\nabla\rho_{\alpha}-q_{\alpha}E+m_{\alpha}\nu_{\alpha}u_{\alpha}=g_{2\alpha},\\ &\partial_{t}E-c\nabla\times B+4\pi\sum_{\alpha=i,e}q_{\alpha}u_{\alpha}=g_{3},\\ &\partial_{t}B+c\nabla\times E=0,\\ &\nabla\cdot E=4\pi\sum_{\alpha=i,e}q_{\alpha}\rho_{\alpha},\ \ \nabla\cdot B=0.\end{aligned}\right. (3.1)

Initial data are given by

[ρα,uα,E,B]|t=0=[nα​0−1,uα​0,E0,B0],\displaystyle[\rho_{\alpha},u_{\alpha},E,B]|_{t=0}=[n_{\alpha 0}-1,u_{\alpha 0},E_{0},B_{0}], (3.2)

with the compatible condition

∇⋅E0=4​π​∑α=i,eqα​ρα​0,∇⋅B0=0.\displaystyle\nabla\cdot E_{0}=4\pi\sum_{\alpha=i,e}q_{\alpha}\rho_{\alpha 0},\ \ \nabla\cdot B_{0}=0. (3.3)

Here the nonhomgeneous source terms are

{g1​α=−∇⋅(ραuα):=∇⋅fα,g2​α=−mαuα⋅∇uα−(pα′​(ρα+1)ρα+1−pα′​(1)1)∇ρα+qαuαc×B,g3=−4π∑α=i,eqαραuα.\left\{\begin{aligned} &g_{1\alpha}=-\nabla\cdot(\rho_{\alpha}u_{\alpha}):=\nabla\cdot f_{\alpha},\\ &g_{2\alpha}=-m_{\alpha}u_{\alpha}\cdot\nabla u_{\alpha}-\left(\frac{p_{\alpha}^{\prime}(\rho_{\alpha}+1)}{\rho_{\alpha}+1}-\frac{p_{\alpha}^{\prime}(1)}{1}\right)\nabla\rho_{\alpha}+q_{\alpha}\frac{u_{\alpha}}{c}\times B,\\ &g_{3}=-4\pi\sum_{\alpha=i,e}q_{\alpha}\rho_{\alpha}u_{\alpha}.\end{aligned}\right. (3.4)

Notice in the isothermal case that pα′​(n)=Tαp_{\alpha}^{\prime}(n)=T_{\alpha} for any n>0n>0.

3.2. Linear decay structure

In this section, for brevity of presentation we still use U=[ρα,uα,E,B]U=[\rho_{\alpha},u_{\alpha},E,B] to denote the solution to the linearized homogeneous system

{∂tρα+∇⋅uα=0,mα∂tuα+Tα∇ρα−qαE+mαναuα=0,∂tE−c∇×B+4π∑α=i,eqαuα=0,∂tB+c∇×E=0,∇⋅E=4π∑α=i,eqαρα,∇⋅B=0,\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}\rho_{\alpha}+\nabla\cdot u_{\alpha}=0,\\ &m_{\alpha}\partial_{t}u_{\alpha}+T_{\alpha}\nabla\rho_{\alpha}-q_{\alpha}E+m_{\alpha}\nu_{\alpha}u_{\alpha}=0,\\ &\partial_{t}E-c\nabla\times B+4\pi\sum_{\alpha=i,e}q_{\alpha}u_{\alpha}=0,\\ &\partial_{t}B+c\nabla\times E=0,\\ &\nabla\cdot E=4\pi\sum_{\alpha=i,e}q_{\alpha}\rho_{\alpha},\ \ \nabla\cdot B=0,\end{aligned}\right. (3.5)

with given initial data

[ρα,uα,E,B]|t=0=[ρα​0,uα​0,E0,B0],\displaystyle[\rho_{\alpha},u_{\alpha},E,B]|_{t=0}=[\rho_{\alpha 0},u_{\alpha 0},E_{0},B_{0}], (3.6)

satisfying the compatible condition

∇⋅E0=4​π​∑α=i,eqα​ρα​0,∇⋅B0=0.\displaystyle\nabla\cdot E_{0}=4\pi\sum_{\alpha=i,e}q_{\alpha}\rho_{\alpha 0},\ \ \nabla\cdot B_{0}=0. (3.7)

The goal of this section is to apply the Fourier energy method to the Cauchy problem (3.5), (3.6), (3.7) to show that there exists a time-frequency Lyapunov functional which is equivalent with |U^​(t,k)|2|\hat{U}(t,k)|^{2} and moreover its dissipation rate can also be characterized by the functional itself. Let us state the main result of this section as follows.

Theorem 3.1.

Let U⁡(t,x)U(t,x), t>0t>0, x∈ℝ3x\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, be a well-defined solution to the system (3.5)-(3.7). There is a time-frequency Lyapunov functional ℰ​(U^​(t,k))\mathcal{E}(\hat{U}(t,k)) with

ℰ⁡(U^​(t,k))∼|U^2|:=∑α=i,e|[ρ^α,u^α]|2+|E^|2+|B^|2,\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\hat{U}(t,k))\sim|\hat{U}^{2}|:=\sum_{\alpha=i,e}|[\hat{\rho}_{\alpha},\hat{u}_{\alpha}]|^{2}+|\hat{E}|^{2}+|\hat{B}|^{2}, (3.8)

such that, for some λ>0\lambda>0, the Lyapunov inequality

dd​t​ℰ​(U^​(t,k))+λ​|k|2(1+|k|2)2​ℰ​(U^​(t,k))≤0\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{E}(\hat{U}(t,k))+\dfrac{\lambda|k|^{2}}{(1+|k|^{2})^{2}}\mathcal{E}(\hat{U}(t,k))\leq 0 (3.9)

holds for any t>0t>0 and k∈ℝ3k\in\mathbb{R}^{3}.

Theorem 3.1 directly leads to the pointwise time-frequency estimate on the modular |U^​(t,k)||\hat{U}(t,k)| in terms of initial data modular |U^0​(k)||\hat{U}_{0}(k)|, which is the same as [6, Corollary 4.1].

Corollary 3.1.

Let U⁡(t,x)U(t,x), t≥0t\geq 0, x∈ℝ3x\in\mathbb{R}^{3} be a well-defined solution to the system (3.5)-(3.7). Then, there are λ>0\lambda>0, C>0C>0 such that

|U^​(t,k)|≤C​exp⁡(−λ​|k|2​t(1+|k|2)2)​|U0^​(k)|\displaystyle|\hat{U}(t,k)|\leq C{\exp\left({-\tfrac{\lambda|k|^{2}t}{(1+|k|^{2})^{2}}}\right)}|\hat{U_{0}}(k)| (3.17)

holds for any t≥0t\geq 0 and k∈ℝ3k\in\mathbb{R}^{3}.

Based on the pointwise time-frequency estimate (3.17), it is also straightforward to obtain the LpL^{p}-LqL^{q} time-decay property to the Cauchy problem (3.5)-(3.6). Formally, the solution to the Cauchy problem (3.5)-(3.6) is denoted by

U⁡(t)=[ρα,uα,E,B]=et​L​U0,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} U(t)=\left[\rho_{\alpha},u_{\alpha},E,B\right]={e^{tL}}U_{0},\end{aligned}

where et​L{e^{tL}} for t≥0t\geq 0 is said to be the linearized solution operator corresponding to the linearized Euler-Maxwell system.

Corollary 3.2 (see [6] for instance).

(3.18)

where [⋅]−[\cdot]_{-} denotes the integer part of the argument. Suppose U0U_{0} satisfying (3.7). Then et​Le^{tL} satisfies the following time-decay property:

‖∇meL​t​U0‖Lq≤C​(1+t)−32​(1p−1q)−m2‖U0‖Lp+C​(1+t)−ℓ2​‖∇m+[ℓ+3​(1r−1q)]+U0‖Lr\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \|\nabla^{m}e^{Lt}U_{0}\|_{L^{q}}\leq C(1+t)^{-\tfrac{3}{2}(\tfrac{1}{p}-\tfrac{1}{q})-\tfrac{m}{2}}&\|U_{0}\|_{L^{p}}\\ +&C(1+t)^{-\tfrac{\ell}{2}}\|\nabla^{m+[\ell+3(\tfrac{1}{r}-\tfrac{1}{q})]_{+}}{U}_{0}\|_{L^{r}}\end{aligned}

for any t≥0t\geq 0, where C=C⁡(m,p,r,q,ℓ)C=C(m,p,r,q,\ell).

4. Spectral representation

In order to study the more accurate large-time asymptotic profile, we need to carry out the spectral analysis of the linearized system.

4.1. Preparations

As in [6], the linearized system (3.5) can be written as two decoupled subsystems which govern the time evolution of ρα\rho_{\alpha}, ∇⋅uα\nabla\cdot u_{\alpha}, ∇⋅E\nabla\cdot E and ∇×uα\nabla\times u_{\alpha}, ∇×E\nabla\times E and ∇×B\nabla\times B respectively. We decompose the solution to (3.5)-(3.7) into two parts in the form of

[ρα​(t,x)uα​(t,x)E⁡(t,x)B⁡(t,x)]=[ρα​(t,x)uα,∥(t,x)E∥​(t,x)0]+[0uα,⟂​(t,x)E⟂​(t,x)B⁡(t,x)],\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\rho_{\alpha}(t,x)\\ u_{\alpha}(t,x)\\ E(t,x)\\ B(t,x)\\ \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\rho_{\alpha}(t,x)\\ u_{\alpha,\parallel}(t,x)\\ E_{\parallel}(t,x)\\ 0\\ \end{array}\right]+\left[\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ u_{\alpha,\perp}(t,x)\\ E_{\perp}(t,x)\\ B(t,x)\\ \end{array}\right],

where uα,∥u_{\alpha,\parallel}, uα,⟂u_{\alpha,\perp} are defined by

uα,∥=−(−Δ)−1∇∇⋅uα,uα,⟂=(−Δ)−1∇×(∇×uα),u_{\alpha,\parallel}=-(-\Delta)^{-1}\nabla\nabla\cdot u_{\alpha},\ \ \ u_{\alpha,\perp}=(-\Delta)^{-1}\nabla\times(\nabla\times u_{\alpha}),

and likewise for E∥E_{\parallel}, E⟂E_{\perp}. For brevity, the first part on the right of (4.1) is called the fluid part and the second part is called the electromagnetic part, and we also write

U∥=[ρi,ρe,ui,∥,ue,∥],U⟂=[ui,⟂,ue,⟂,E⟂,B].U_{\parallel}=[\rho_{i},\rho_{e},u_{i,\parallel},u_{e,\parallel}],\quad U_{\perp}=[u_{i,\perp},u_{e,\perp},E_{\perp},B].

Notice that to the end, E∥E_{\parallel} is always given by

E∥=4πeΔ−1∇(ρi−ρe).E_{\parallel}=4\pi e\Delta^{-1}\nabla(\rho_{i}-\rho_{e}).

We now derive the equations of U∥U_{\parallel} and U⟂U_{\perp} and their asymptotic equations that one may expect in the large time. Taking the divergence of the second equation of (3.5), it follows that

{∂tρα+∇⋅uα=0,mα∂t(∇⋅uα)−qα∇⋅E+TαΔρα+mανα∇⋅uα=0.\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}\rho_{\alpha}+\nabla\cdot u_{\alpha}=0,\\ &m_{\alpha}\partial_{t}(\nabla\cdot u_{\alpha})-q_{\alpha}\nabla\cdot E+T_{\alpha}\Delta\rho_{\alpha}+m_{\alpha}\nu_{\alpha}\nabla\cdot u_{\alpha}=0.\\ \end{aligned}\right. (4.14)

Applying Δ−1∇\Delta^{-1}\nabla to the second equation of (4.14) and noticing ∇⋅uα=∇⋅uα,∥\nabla\cdot u_{\alpha}=\nabla\cdot u_{\alpha,\parallel}, we see that the fluid part U∥U_{\parallel} satisfies

{∂tρα+∇⋅uα,∥=0,mα∂tuα,∥−qαE∥+Tα∇ρα+mαναuα,∥=0.\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}\rho_{\alpha}+\nabla\cdot u_{\alpha,\parallel}=0,\\ &m_{\alpha}\partial_{t}u_{\alpha,\parallel}-q_{\alpha}E_{\parallel}+T_{\alpha}\nabla\rho_{\alpha}+m_{\alpha}\nu_{\alpha}u_{\alpha,\parallel}=0.\\ \end{aligned}\right. [ρα,uα,∥]|t=0=[ρα​0,uα0,∥].[\rho_{\alpha},\ u_{\alpha,\parallel}]|_{t=0}=[\rho_{\alpha 0},\ u_{\alpha 0,\parallel}]. (4.16)

As seen later on and also in the sense of the Darcy’s law, the expected asymptotic profile of the fluid part satisfies

The electromagnetic part satisfies the following equations:

At this time, although we have known that there is at least one real root, it is not clear whether these roots are distinct or not. We can distinguish several possible cases using the discriminant,

Δ=18​c2​c1​c0−4​c23​c0+c22​c12−4​c13−27​c02.\Delta=18c_{2}c_{1}c_{0}-4c_{2}^{3}c_{0}+c_{2}^{2}c_{1}^{2}-4c_{1}^{3}-27c_{0}^{2}.

    Δ>0\Delta>0, then g⁡(λ)=0g(\lambda)=0 has three distinct real roots;

4.3.2. Error estimates

In this section, we first give the error estimates for B−B¯{B}-\bar{B}, and then apply the energy method in the Fourier space to the difference problem for (4.21) and (4.23) to get the error estimates for uα,⟂−u¯α,⟂u_{\alpha,\perp}-\bar{u}_{\alpha,\perp} and E⟂−E¯⟂E_{\perp}-\bar{E}_{\perp}. It should be pointed out that it is also possible to carry out the same strenuous procedure as in the previous section to obtain the error estimates on uα,⟂−u¯α,⟂u_{\alpha,\perp}-\bar{u}_{\alpha,\perp} and Eα,⟂−E¯α,⟂E_{\alpha,\perp}-\bar{E}_{\alpha,\perp}. The reason why we choose the Fourier energy method is just for the simplicity of representation, since the estimates on uα,⟂−u¯α,⟂u_{\alpha,\perp}-\bar{u}_{\alpha,\perp} and Eα,⟂−E¯α,⟂E_{\alpha,\perp}-\bar{E}_{\alpha,\perp} can be directly obtained basing on the estimate on B−B¯{B}-\bar{B}.

Lemma 4.3.

There is r0>0r_{0}>0 such that for |k|≤r0|k|\leq r_{0} and t≥0t\geq 0,

|B^​(t,k)−B¯^​(t,k)|≤C⁡(|k|​exp⁡(−λ​|k|2​t)+exp⁡(−λ​t))​|U^0,⟂|,\displaystyle|\hat{B}(t,k)-\hat{\bar{B}}(t,k)|\leq C\left(|k|{\exp({-\lambda|k|^{2}t})+\exp({-\lambda t})}\right)|\hat{U}_{0,\perp}|, (4.66)

where CC and λ\lambda are positive constants.

Proof.

It follows from (4.45) and (4.25) that

B^​(t,k)−B¯^​(t,k)=∑j=14cj​(i​k)​exp⁡{λj​(i​k)​t}−exp⁡(−c2​mi​νi​me​νe4​π​e2​(mi​νi+me​νe)​|k|2​t)​B^0​(k)=(c1​(i​k)−B^0)​exp⁡{λ1​(i​k)​t}+B^0​(exp⁡{λ1​(i​k)​t}−exp⁡{−c2​mi​νi​me​νe4​π​e2​(mi​νi+me​νe)​|k|2​t})+∑j=24exp{λj(ik)t}cj(ik):⁣=R^21​(i​k)+R^22​(i​k)+R^23​(i​k).\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \hat{B}(t,k)-\hat{\bar{B}}(t,k)=&\sum_{j=1}^{4}c_{j}(ik)\exp\{\lambda_{j}(ik)t\}-\exp\left(-\dfrac{c^{2}m_{i}\nu_{i}m_{e}\nu_{e}}{4\pi e^{2}(m_{i}\nu_{i}+m_{e}\nu_{e})}|k|^{2}t\right)\hat{B}_{0}(k)\\ =&(c_{1}(ik)-\hat{B}_{0}){\exp\{\lambda_{1}(ik)t\}}+\hat{B}_{0}\left(\exp\{\lambda_{1}(ik)t\}-\exp\left\{-\dfrac{c^{2}m_{i}\nu_{i}m_{e}\nu_{e}}{4\pi e^{2}(m_{i}\nu_{i}+m_{e}\nu_{e})}|k|^{2}t\right\}\right)\\ &+\sum_{j=2}^{4}\exp\{\lambda_{j}(ik)t\}c_{j}(ik)\\ :=&\hat{R}_{21}(ik)+\hat{R}_{22}(ik)+\hat{R}_{23}(ik).\end{aligned}

Using (4.44) and (4.65), one has

|R^21​(i​k)|\displaystyle|\hat{R}_{21}(ik)| ≤\displaystyle\leq C​|k|​exp⁡(−λ​|k|2​t)​|U^0,⟂|,\displaystyle C|k|{\exp({-\lambda|k|^{2}t})}|\hat{U}_{0,\perp}|,
|R^22​(i​k)|\displaystyle|\hat{R}_{22}(ik)| ≤\displaystyle\leq C​|k|2​exp⁡(−λ​|k|2​t)​|B^0|,\displaystyle C|k|^{2}{\exp({-\lambda|k|^{2}t})}|\hat{B}_{0}|,
|R^23​(i​k)|\displaystyle|\hat{R}_{23}(ik)| ≤\displaystyle\leq C​exp⁡(−λ​t)​|U^0,⟂|.\displaystyle C{\exp({-\lambda t})}|\hat{U}_{0,\perp}|.

This proves (4.66) and then completes the proof of Lemma 4.3. ∎

Next, in order to get the error estimates for uα,⟂−u¯α,⟂u_{\alpha,\perp}-\bar{u}_{\alpha,\perp} and E⟂−E¯⟂E_{\perp}-\bar{E}_{\perp}, we write

Combining (4.21) with (4.23), then [u~α,E~][\tilde{u}_{\alpha},\tilde{E}] satisfies

{mα∂tu~α−qαE~+mαναu~α=−mα∂tu¯α,⟂,∂tE~−c∇×B~+4π∑α=i,eqαu~α=−∂tE¯⟂.\left\{\begin{aligned} &m_{\alpha}\partial_{t}\tilde{u}_{\alpha}-q_{\alpha}\tilde{E}+m_{\alpha}\nu_{\alpha}\tilde{u}_{\alpha}=-m_{\alpha}\partial_{t}\bar{u}_{\alpha,\perp},\\ &\partial_{t}\tilde{E}-c\nabla\times\tilde{B}+4\pi\sum_{\alpha=i,e}q_{\alpha}\tilde{u}_{\alpha}=-\partial_{t}\bar{E}_{\perp}.\\ \end{aligned}\right. (4.67)
Lemma 4.4.

There is r0>0r_{0}>0 such that

|u^α,⟂(t,k)−u¯^α,⟂(t,k)|≤{(C​|k|2​exp⁡(−λ​|k|2​t)+exp⁡(−λ​t))​|U^0,⟂|,for​|k|≤r0,C​exp⁡(−λ​|k|−2​t)​|U^0​(k)|+C​exp⁡(−λ​|k|2​t)|k||B^0​(k)|,for|k|≥r0,\displaystyle|\hat{u}_{\alpha,\perp}(t,k)-\hat{\bar{u}}_{\alpha,\perp}(t,k)|\leq\left\{\begin{aligned} &\left(C|k|^{2}{\exp({-\lambda|k|^{2}t})}+{\exp({-\lambda t})}\right)|\hat{U}_{0,\perp}|,\ \ \ \mathrm{for}\ |k|\leq r_{0},\\ &\begin{aligned} &C\exp{\left(-\lambda|k|^{-2}t\right)}\left|\hat{U}_{0}(k)\right|\\ &\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ +C\exp{\left(-\lambda|k|^{2}t\right)}|k|\left|\hat{B}_{0}(k)\right|,\ \mathrm{for}\ |k|\geq r_{0},\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\right. (4.68)

and

|E^⟂(t,k)−E¯^⟂(t,k)|≤{(C​|k|2​exp⁡(−λ​|k|2​t)+exp⁡(−λ​t))​|U^0,⟂|,for​|k|≤r0,C​exp⁡(−λ​|k|−2​t)​|U^0​(k)|+C​exp⁡(−λ​|k|2​t)|k||B^0​(k)|,for|k|≥r0,\displaystyle|\hat{E}_{\perp}(t,k)-\hat{\bar{E}}_{\perp}(t,k)|\leq\left\{\begin{aligned} &\left(C|k|^{2}{\exp({-\lambda|k|^{2}t})}+{\exp({-\lambda t})}\right)|\hat{U}_{0,\perp}|,\ \ \ \mathrm{for}\ |k|\leq r_{0},\\ &\begin{aligned} &C\exp{\left(-\lambda|k|^{-2}t\right)}\left|\hat{U}_{0}(k)\right|\\ &\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ +C\exp{\left(-\lambda|k|^{2}t\right)}|k|\left|\hat{B}_{0}(k)\right|,\ \mathrm{for}\ |k|\geq r_{0},\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\right. (4.69)

where CC and λ\lambda are positive constants.

Proof.

It is straightforward to obtain the error estimates for |k|≥r0|k|\geq r_{0} due to (3.17), (4.24) and (4.25). In the case |k|≤r0|k|\leq r_{0}, the desired result can follow from the Fourier energy estimate on the system (4.67). Indeed, after taking the Fourier transform in xx, (4.67) gives

{mα∂tu~^α−qαE~^+mαναu~^α=−mα∂tu¯^α,⟂,∂tE~^−cik×B~^+4π∑α=i,eqαu~^α=−∂tE¯^⟂.\left\{\begin{aligned} &m_{\alpha}\partial_{t}\hat{\tilde{u}}_{\alpha}-q_{\alpha}\hat{\tilde{E}}+m_{\alpha}\nu_{\alpha}\hat{\tilde{u}}_{\alpha}=-m_{\alpha}\partial_{t}\hat{\bar{u}}_{\alpha,\perp},\\ &\partial_{t}\hat{\tilde{E}}-cik\times\hat{\tilde{B}}+4\pi\sum_{\alpha=i,e}q_{\alpha}\hat{\tilde{u}}_{\alpha}=-\partial_{t}\hat{\bar{E}}_{\perp}.\\ \end{aligned}\right. which by using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality with 0<ϵ<10<\epsilon<1, implies

12​dd​t​(∑α=i,emα​|u~^α|2+14​π​|E~^|2)+∑α=i,emα​να​|u~^α|2≤ϵ​∑α=i,e|u~^α|2+ϵ​|E~^|2+Cϵ​∑α=i,e|∂tu¯^α,⟂|2+Cϵ​|i​k×B~^|2+Cϵ​|∂tE¯^⟂|2.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\left(\sum_{\alpha=i,e}m_{\alpha}|\hat{\tilde{u}}_{\alpha}|^{2}+\frac{1}{4\pi}|\hat{\tilde{E}}|^{2}\right)+\sum_{\alpha=i,e}m_{\alpha}\nu_{\alpha}|\hat{\tilde{u}}_{\alpha}|^{2}\\ \leq&\epsilon\sum_{\alpha=i,e}|\hat{\tilde{u}}_{\alpha}|^{2}+\epsilon|\hat{\tilde{E}}|^{2}+C_{\epsilon}\sum_{\alpha=i,e}|\partial_{t}\hat{\bar{u}}_{\alpha,\perp}|^{2}+C_{\epsilon}|ik\times\hat{\tilde{B}}|^{2}+C_{\epsilon}|\partial_{t}\hat{\bar{E}}_{\perp}|^{2}.\end{aligned} (4.71)

Theorem 4.2.

Let 1≤p,r≤2≤q≤∞1\leq p,r\leq 2\leq q\leq\infty, ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0, and let m≥1m\geq 1 be an integer. Suppose that U⟂=[uα,⟂,E⟂,B]U_{\perp}=[u_{\alpha,\perp},E_{\perp},B] is the solution to the Cauchy problem (4.21)-(4.22). Then one has the following time-decay property:

‖∇m(E⟂​(t)−E¯⟂​(t))‖Lq≤C​(1+t)−32​(1p−1q)−m+22​‖U0‖Lp+C​exp⁡(−λ​t)​‖U0‖Lp+C​(1+t)−ℓ2​‖∇m+[ℓ+3​(1r−1q)]+U0‖Lr+C​exp⁡(−λ​t)​‖∇m+1+[3​(1r−1q)]+B0‖Lr,\|\nabla^{m}(E_{\perp}(t)-\bar{E}_{\perp}(t))\|_{L^{q}}\leq C(1+t)^{-\frac{3}{2}(\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q})-\frac{m+2}{2}}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{p}}+C{\exp({-\lambda t})}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{p}}\\ +C(1+t)^{-\frac{\ell}{2}}\|\nabla^{m+[\ell+3(\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{q})]_{+}}U_{0}\|_{L^{r}}+C{\exp({-\lambda t})}\|\nabla^{m+1+[3(\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{q})]_{+}}B_{0}\|_{L^{r}},

and

‖∇m(B⁡(t)−B¯​(t))‖Lq≤C​(1+t)−32​(1p−1q)−m+12​‖U0‖Lp+C​exp⁡(−λ​t)​‖U0‖Lp+C​(1+t)−ℓ2​‖∇m+[ℓ+3​(1r−1q)]+U0‖Lr+C​exp⁡(−λ​t)​‖∇m+[3​(1r−1q)]+B0‖Lr,\|\nabla^{m}(B(t)-\bar{B}(t))\|_{L^{q}}\leq C(1+t)^{-\frac{3}{2}(\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q})-\frac{m+1}{2}}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{p}}+C{\exp({-\lambda t})}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{p}}\\ +C(1+t)^{-\frac{\ell}{2}}\|\nabla^{m+[\ell+3(\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{q})]_{+}}U_{0}\|_{L^{r}}+C{\exp({-\lambda t})}\|\nabla^{m+[3(\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{q})]_{+}}B_{0}\|_{L^{r}},

for any t≥0t\geq 0, where C=C⁡(m,p,r,q,ℓ)C=C(m,p,r,q,\ell) and [ℓ+3​(1r−1q)]+[\ell+3(\tfrac{1}{r}-\tfrac{1}{q})]_{+} is defined in (3.18).

We now define the expected time-asymptotic profile of [ρα,uα,E,B][\rho_{\alpha},u_{\alpha},E,B] to be [ρ¯,u¯α,E¯,B¯][\bar{\rho},\bar{u}_{\alpha},\bar{E},\bar{B}], where ρ¯\bar{\rho} and B¯\bar{B} are diffusion waves, and [u¯α,E¯][\bar{u}_{\alpha},\bar{E}] is given by

u¯α=u¯∥+u¯α,⟂,E¯=E¯∥+E¯⟂.\displaystyle\bar{u}_{\alpha}=\bar{u}_{\parallel}+\bar{u}_{\alpha,\perp},\ \ \ \ \ \bar{E}=\bar{E}_{\parallel}+\bar{E}_{\perp}.

Combining Theorem 4.1 with Theorem 4.2, one has

Corollary 4.1.

Let 1≤p,r≤2≤q≤∞1\leq p,r\leq 2\leq q\leq\infty, ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0, and let m≥1m\geq 1 be an integer. and if ϵN+6​(U0)\epsilon_{N+6}(U_{0}) is sufficiently small then

‖∇U​(t)‖N−1≤C​ϵN+6​(U0)​(1+t)−54.\displaystyle\|\nabla U(t)\|_{N-1}\leq C\epsilon_{N+6}(U_{0})(1+t)^{-\frac{5}{4}}.

Now, we write down the L2L^{2} time-decay rates of [ρα,B][\rho_{\alpha},B] and [uα,E][u_{\alpha},E] as follows.

Estimate on ‖[ρα,B]‖L2\|[\rho_{\alpha},B]\|_{L^{2}}. It is easy to see from (5.36) that

‖B⁡(t)‖+∑i=i,e‖ρα‖≤C​ϵ5​(U0)​(1+t)−34.\displaystyle\|B(t)\|+\sum_{i=i,e}\|\rho_{\alpha}\|\leq C\epsilon_{5}(U_{0})(1+t)^{-\frac{3}{4}}. (5.37)

Estimate on ‖[uα,E]‖L2\|[u_{\alpha},E]\|_{L^{2}}. Applying the second and the third linear estimate on [uα,E][u_{\alpha},E] with m=0,q=r=2,p=1,ℓ=5/2m=0,\ q=r=2,\ p=1,\ \ell=5/2 in Corollary 4.2 to the mild form (4.76), one has

‖[uα,E]​(t)‖≤C​(1+t)−54​‖U0‖L1∩H˙3+exp⁡{−λ​t}​‖∇[ρi​0,ρe​0,B0]‖+C∫0t(1+t−s)−54∥[g1​α(s),g2​α(s),g3(s)]∥L1∩H˙3ds+C∫0texp{−λ(t−s)}∥∇[g1​i(s),g1​e(s)]∥ds.\|[u_{\alpha},E](t)\|\leq C(1+t)^{-\frac{5}{4}}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{1}\cap\dot{H}^{3}}+{\exp\{-\lambda t\}}\|\nabla[\rho_{i0},\rho_{e0},B_{0}]\|\\ +C\int_{0}^{t}(1+t-s)^{-\frac{5}{4}}\|[g_{1\alpha}(s),g_{2\alpha}(s),g_{3}(s)]\|_{L^{1}\cap\dot{H}^{3}}ds\\ +C\int_{0}^{t}{\exp\{-\lambda(t-s)\}}\|\nabla[g_{1i}(s),g_{1e}(s)]\|ds.

By (5.36), it follows that

‖∇[g1​i​(s),g1​e​(s)]‖+‖[g1​α​(s),g2​α​(s),g3​(s)]‖L1∩H˙3≤C​‖U⁡(t)‖42≤C​ϵ62​(U0)​(1+t)−32.\|\nabla[g_{1i}(s),g_{1e}(s)]\|+\|[g_{1\alpha}(s),g_{2\alpha}(s),g_{3}(s)]\|_{L^{1}\cap\dot{H}^{3}}\leq C\|U(t)\|^{2}_{4}\leq C\epsilon_{6}^{2}(U_{0})(1+t)^{-\frac{3}{2}}.

Therefore, one has

‖[uα,E]​(t)‖≤C​ϵ6​(U0)​(1+t)−54.\displaystyle\|[u_{\alpha},E](t)\|\leq C\epsilon_{6}(U_{0})(1+t)^{-\frac{5}{4}}. (5.38)

5.3. Asymptotic rate to diffusion waves

In this section we shall prove the main Theorem 1.1 on the large-time asymptotic behavior of the obtained solutions.

First of all, we prove in the following lemma that the solution U⁡(x,t)=[ρα,uα,E,B]U(x,t)=[\rho_{\alpha},u_{\alpha},E,B] to the nonlinear Cauchy problem (3.1)-(3.3) can be approximated by the one of the corresponding linearized problem (3.5)-(3.7) in large time.

Lemma 5.5.

Suppose that ϵ11​(U0)>0\epsilon_{11}(U_{0})>0 is sufficiently small, and U⁡(x,t)=[ρα,uα,E,B]U(x,t)=[\rho_{\alpha},u_{\alpha},E,B] is a solution to the Cauchy problem (3.1)-(3.3) with initial data U0U_{0}. Then it holds that

‖ρα​(t)−𝐏1​α​et​L​U0‖≤C​(1+t)−54,\displaystyle\left\|\rho_{\alpha}(t)-\mathbf{P}_{1\alpha}e^{tL}U_{0}\right\|\leq C(1+t)^{-\frac{5}{4}}, (5.39)
‖uα​(t)−𝐏2​α​et​L​U0‖≤C​(1+t)−74,\displaystyle\left\|u_{\alpha}(t)-\mathbf{P}_{2\alpha}e^{tL}U_{0}\right\|\leq C(1+t)^{-\frac{7}{4}}, (5.40)
‖E⁡(t)−𝐏3​et​L​U0‖≤C​(1+t)−74,\displaystyle\left\|E(t)-\mathbf{P}_{3}e^{tL}U_{0}\right\|\leq C(1+t)^{-\frac{7}{4}}, (5.41)
‖B⁡(t)−𝐏4​et​L​U0‖≤C​(1+t)−54,\displaystyle\left\|B(t)-\mathbf{P}_{4}e^{tL}U_{0}\right\|\leq C(1+t)^{-\frac{5}{4}}, (5.42)

for any t≥0t\geq 0.

Proof.

We rewrite each component of solutions U⁡(x,t)=[ρα,uα,E,B]U(x,t)=[\rho_{\alpha},u_{\alpha},E,B] to (3.1) as the mild forms by the Duhamel’s principle:

ρα​(x,t)=𝐏1​α​et​L​U0+∫0t𝐏1​α​e(t−s)​L​[∇⋅fα​(s),g2​α​(s),g3​(s),0]​𝑑s,\rho_{\alpha}(x,t)=\mathbf{P}_{1\alpha}e^{tL}U_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\mathbf{P}_{1\alpha}e^{(t-s)L}[\nabla\cdot f_{\alpha}(s),g_{2\alpha}(s),g_{3}(s),0]ds, (5.43)
uα​(x,t)=𝐏2​α​et​L​U0+∫0t𝐏2​α​e(t−s)​L​[∇⋅fα​(s),g2​α​(s),g3​(s),0]​𝑑s,u_{\alpha}(x,t)=\mathbf{P}_{2\alpha}e^{tL}U_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\mathbf{P}_{2\alpha}e^{(t-s)L}[\nabla\cdot f_{\alpha}(s),g_{2\alpha}(s),g_{3}(s),0]ds, (5.44)

for α=i,e\alpha=i,e, and

E⁡(x,t)=𝐏3​et​L​U0+∫0t𝐏3​e(t−s)​L​[∇⋅fα​(s),g2​α​(s),g3​(s),0]​𝑑s,E(x,t)=\mathbf{P}_{3}e^{tL}U_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\mathbf{P}_{3}e^{(t-s)L}[\nabla\cdot f_{\alpha}(s),g_{2\alpha}(s),g_{3}(s),0]ds,
B⁡(x,t)=𝐏4​et​L​U0+∫0t𝐏4​e(t−s)​L​[∇⋅fα​(s),g2​α​(s),g3​(s),0]​𝑑s.B(x,t)=\mathbf{P}_{4}e^{tL}U_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\mathbf{P}_{4}e^{(t-s)L}[\nabla\cdot f_{\alpha}(s),g_{2\alpha}(s),g_{3}(s),0]ds.

Denote N⁡(s)=[∇⋅fα​(s),g2​α​(s),g3​(s),0]N(s)=[\nabla\cdot f_{\alpha}(s),g_{2\alpha}(s),g_{3}(s),0] as in Section 4.4. In what follows we only prove (5.39) and (5.40), and the other two estimates (5.41) and (5.42) can be proved in a similar way. One can apply the linear estimate on 𝐏1​α​et​L​N0\mathbf{P}_{1\alpha}e^{tL}N_{0} to the mild form (5.43) by letting m=0,q=r=2,p=1,ℓ=5/2m=0,\ q=r=2,\ p=1,\ \ell=5/2 in Theorem 4.3, so as to obtain

‖ρα​(t)−𝐏1​α​et​L​U0‖≤∫0t‖𝐏1​α​e(t−s)​L​[∇⋅fα​(s),g2​α​(s),g3​(s),0]‖​𝑑s≤C​∫0t(1+t−s)−54​(‖N⁡(s)‖L1∩H˙3+‖[fi,fe]​(s)‖L1)+exp⁡{λ⁡(t−s)}​‖∇[fi,fe]​(s)‖​ds.\left\|\rho_{\alpha}(t)-\mathbf{P}_{1\alpha}e^{tL}U_{0}\right\|\leq\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}\left\|\mathbf{P}_{1\alpha}e^{(t-s)L}[\nabla\cdot f_{\alpha}(s),g_{2\alpha}(s),g_{3}(s),0]\right\|ds\\ \leq C\int_{0}^{t}(1+t-s)^{-\frac{5}{4}}\left(\|N(s)\|_{L^{1}\cap\dot{H}^{3}}+\|[f_{i},f_{e}](s)\|_{L^{1}}\right)+{\exp\{\lambda(t-s)\}}\|\nabla[f_{i},f_{e}](s)\|ds. (5.45)

Recalling the definition (3.4), it is straightforward to verify

‖N⁡(s)‖L1∩H˙3+‖[fi,fe]​(s)‖L1≤C​‖U⁡(s)‖42≤C​ϵ62​(U0)​(1+s)−32,\displaystyle\|N(s)\|_{L^{1}\cap\dot{H}^{3}}+\|[f_{i},f_{e}](s)\|_{L^{1}}\leq C\|U(s)\|_{4}^{2}\leq C\epsilon_{6}^{2}(U_{0})(1+s)^{-\frac{3}{2}},

and

‖∇[fi,fe]​(s)‖≤C​‖U⁡(s)‖42≤C​ϵ62​(U0)​(1+s)−32.\displaystyle\|\nabla[f_{i},f_{e}](s)\|\leq C\|U(s)\|_{4}^{2}\leq C\epsilon_{6}^{2}(U_{0})(1+s)^{-\frac{3}{2}}.

Plugging these estimates into (5.45), it follows that

‖ρα​(t)−𝐏1​α​et​L​U0‖≤C​(1+t)−54.\left\|\rho_{\alpha}(t)-\mathbf{P}_{1\alpha}e^{tL}U_{0}\right\|\leq C(1+t)^{-\frac{5}{4}}.

Applying the linear estimate on 𝐏2​α​et​L​N0\mathbf{P}_{2\alpha}e^{tL}N_{0} to the mild form (5.44) by letting m=0,q=r=2,p=1,ℓ=7/2m=0,\ q=r=2,\ p=1,\ \ell=7/2 in Theorem 4.3 gives

‖uα​(t)−𝐏2​α​et​L​U0‖≤∫0t‖𝐏2​α​e(t−s)​L​[∇⋅fα​(s),g2​α​(s),g3​(s),0]‖​𝑑s≤C​∫0t(1+t−s)−74​(‖N⁡(s)‖L1∩H˙4+‖[fi,fe]​(s)‖L1)+exp⁡{λ⁡(t−s)}​‖∇2[fi,fe]​(s)‖​ds.\left\|u_{\alpha}(t)-\mathbf{P}_{2\alpha}e^{tL}U_{0}\right\|\leq\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}\left\|\mathbf{P}_{2\alpha}e^{(t-s)L}[\nabla\cdot f_{\alpha}(s),g_{2\alpha}(s),g_{3}(s),0]\right\|ds\\ \leq C\int_{0}^{t}(1+t-s)^{-\frac{7}{4}}\left(\|N(s)\|_{L^{1}\cap\dot{H}^{4}}+\|[f_{i},f_{e}](s)\|_{L^{1}}\right)+{\exp\{\lambda(t-s)\}}\|\nabla^{2}[f_{i},f_{e}](s)\|ds. (5.46)

As before, recall the definition (3.4) and the time-decay rates (5.37) and (5.38). We first estimate L1L^{1} norms of those terms without any derivative as

‖uα×B‖L1≤‖uα‖​‖B‖≤C​ϵ62​(U0)​(1+s)−54​(1+s)−34≤C​ϵ62​(U0)​(1+s)−2,‖ρα​uα‖L1≤‖uα‖​‖ρα‖≤C​ϵ62​(U0)​(1+s)−54​(1+s)−34≤C​ϵ62​(U0)​(1+s)−2,‖fα​(s)‖L1≤‖uα‖​‖ρα‖≤C​ϵ62​(U0)​(1+s)−54​(1+s)−34≤C​ϵ62​(U0)​(1+s)−2.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\|u_{\alpha}\times B\|_{L^{1}}\leq\|u_{\alpha}\|\|B\|\leq C\epsilon_{6}^{2}(U_{0})(1+s)^{-\frac{5}{4}}(1+s)^{-\frac{3}{4}}\leq C\epsilon_{6}^{2}(U_{0})(1+s)^{-2},\\ &\|\rho_{\alpha}u_{\alpha}\|_{L^{1}}\leq\|u_{\alpha}\|\|\rho_{\alpha}\|\leq C\epsilon_{6}^{2}(U_{0})(1+s)^{-\frac{5}{4}}(1+s)^{-\frac{3}{4}}\leq C\epsilon_{6}^{2}(U_{0})(1+s)^{-2},\\ &\|f_{\alpha}(s)\|_{L^{1}}\leq\|u_{\alpha}\|\|\rho_{\alpha}\|\leq C\epsilon_{6}^{2}(U_{0})(1+s)^{-\frac{5}{4}}(1+s)^{-\frac{3}{4}}\leq C\epsilon_{6}^{2}(U_{0})(1+s)^{-2}.\end{aligned}

For other terms with one derivative, for ρα∇⋅uα\rho_{\alpha}\nabla\cdot u_{\alpha}, one has

∥ρα∇⋅uα∥L1≤∥∇uα∥∥ρα∥≤Cϵ9(U0)(1+s)−54ϵ5(U0)(1+s)−34≤Cϵ92(U0)(1+s)−2,\displaystyle\|\rho_{\alpha}\nabla\cdot u_{\alpha}\|_{L^{1}}\leq\|\nabla u_{\alpha}\|\|\rho_{\alpha}\|\leq C\epsilon_{9}(U_{0})(1+s)^{-\frac{5}{4}}\epsilon_{5}(U_{0})(1+s)^{-\frac{3}{4}}\leq C\epsilon_{9}^{2}(U_{0})(1+s)^{-2},

and similarly it follows that

∥uα⋅∇ρα∥L1+∥uα⋅∇uα∥L1+∥ρα∇ρα∥L1≤Cϵ92(U0)(1+s)−2.\displaystyle\|u_{\alpha}\cdot\nabla\rho_{\alpha}\|_{L^{1}}+\|u_{\alpha}\cdot\nabla u_{\alpha}\|_{L^{1}}+\|\rho_{\alpha}\nabla\rho_{\alpha}\|_{L^{1}}\leq C\epsilon_{9}^{2}(U_{0})(1+s)^{-2}.

For L2L^{2} norms, by calculating for |l|=4|l|=4,

‖∂l(uα×B)‖≤‖uα‖L∞​‖∂lB‖+‖B‖L∞​‖∂luα‖≤C​‖∇U‖32≤ϵ102​(U0)​(1+s)−52,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \|\partial^{l}(u_{\alpha}\times B)\|\leq&\|u_{\alpha}\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\partial^{l}B\|+\|B\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\partial^{l}u_{\alpha}\|\leq C\|\nabla U\|_{3}^{2}\leq\epsilon_{10}^{2}(U_{0})(1+s)^{-\frac{5}{2}},\end{aligned}

and

‖∂l(uα⋅∇ρα)‖≤‖uα‖L∞​‖∂l∇ρα‖+‖∇ρα‖L∞​‖∂luα‖≤C​‖∇U‖42≤ϵ112​(U0)​(1+s)−52,\|\partial^{l}(u_{\alpha}\cdot\nabla\rho_{\alpha})\|\leq\|u_{\alpha}\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\partial^{l}\nabla\rho_{\alpha}\|+\|\nabla\rho_{\alpha}\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\partial^{l}u_{\alpha}\|\leq C\|\nabla U\|_{4}^{2}\leq\epsilon_{11}^{2}(U_{0})(1+s)^{-\frac{5}{2}},

it is direct to verify that

‖N⁡(s)‖H˙4+‖∇2[fi,fe]​(s)‖≤C​‖∇U​(s)‖42≤C​ϵ112​(U0)​(1+s)−52.\displaystyle\|N(s)\|_{\dot{H}^{4}}+\|\nabla^{2}[f_{i},f_{e}](s)\|\leq C\|\nabla U(s)\|_{4}^{2}\leq C\epsilon_{11}^{2}(U_{0})(1+s)^{-\frac{5}{2}}.

Plugging the above inequalities into (5.46) gives

‖uα​(t)−𝐏2​α​et​L​U0‖≤C​(1+t)−74.\left\|u_{\alpha}(t)-\mathbf{P}_{2\alpha}e^{tL}U_{0}\right\|\leq C(1+t)^{-\frac{7}{4}}.

This then completes the proof of Lemma 5.5. ∎

For the solution U⁡(x,t)=[ρα,uα,E,B]U(x,t)=[\rho_{\alpha},u_{\alpha},E,B] to the Cauchy problem (3.1)-(3.3) and the desired large-time asymptotic profile U¯​(x,t)=[ρ¯,u¯α,E¯,B¯]\overline{U}(x,t)=[\overline{\rho},\overline{u}_{\alpha},\overline{E},\overline{B}], their difference can be rewritten as

U−U¯=(U−et​L​U0)+(et​L​U0−U¯),U-\overline{U}=(U-e^{tL}U_{0})+(e^{tL}U_{0}-\overline{U}),

that is,

ρα−ρ¯=(ρα−𝐏1​α​et​L​U0)+(𝐏1​α​et​L​U0−ρ¯),\displaystyle\rho_{\alpha}-\overline{\rho}=\left(\rho_{\alpha}-\mathbf{P}_{1\alpha}e^{tL}U_{0}\right)+\left(\mathbf{P}_{1\alpha}e^{tL}U_{0}-\overline{\rho}\right),
uα−u¯α=(uα−𝐏2​α​et​L​U0)+(𝐏2​α​et​L​U0−u¯α),\displaystyle u_{\alpha}-\overline{u}_{\alpha}=\left(u_{\alpha}-\mathbf{P}_{2\alpha}e^{tL}U_{0}\right)+\left(\mathbf{P}_{2\alpha}e^{tL}U_{0}-\overline{u}_{\alpha}\right),
E−E¯=(E−𝐏3​et​L​U0)+(𝐏3​et​L​U0−E¯),\displaystyle E-\overline{E}=\left(E-\mathbf{P}_{3}e^{tL}U_{0}\right)+\left(\mathbf{P}_{3}e^{tL}U_{0}-\overline{E}\right),
B−B¯=(B−𝐏4​et​L​U0)+(𝐏4​et​L​U0−B¯).\displaystyle B-\overline{B}=\left(B-\mathbf{P}_{4}e^{tL}U_{0}\right)+\left(\mathbf{P}_{4}e^{tL}U_{0}-\overline{B}\right).

Therefore Theorem 1.1 follows from Lemma 5.5, Theorem 4.1 and Theorem 4.2. ∎
